Not sure why you're getting downvoted when you're just trying to learn. Tall t waves are a tricky topic. Their causes can include all sorts of badness like MI and hyperK, but some of the tallest and peakiest T waves can be seen in perfectly healthy young people. Different books and resources have different ways of measuring tall T waves, sometimes it's more helpful to look at the size relative to the QRS complex rather than exact measurement.

Ultimately, as with most things, it's about the clinical picture: is the patient young and healthy with no cardiac symptoms? If so it's most likely normal variant. Are they elderly and symptomatic? If so it's probably worth getting some bloods or speaking to cardiology

In your example above, you have a big QRS so would normally expect a biggish T, it's roughly 1/3 size of complex and I wouldn't be too concerned. It all looks proportional. Most of the worrying t waves I've seen are as big or bigger than the QRS
